text: The networking and cybersecurity fundamentals course introduced MITRE ATT&CK as a public, continuously updated knowledge base of real adversary tactics -- the attacker's goal -- and ID-numbered techniques, the specific method. Lesson 25 already named it as one source of hunting hypotheses. This lesson is about using it systematically, not just when a technique happens to come to mind.

Instead of picking one technique at random whenever something comes to mind, work through the matrix tactic by tactic and ask: have we actually hunted for evidence of this one yet? That turns the framework from a reference chart you check after an incident into the thing that tells a hunting program exactly where to go next.

Take Lateral Movement -- an attacker who already has a foothold trying to reach other systems. ATT&CK lists T1021, Remote Services, under that tactic: abusing legitimate tools like RDP or WinRM to hop between machines. That becomes a specific hypothesis -- a compromised account using RDP in a pattern that doesn't match normal admin behavior.

Working through a tactic one technique at a time naturally produces a record of what's been checked. Serious teams track that as coverage, often visualized as a heat map with the free MITRE ATT&CK Navigator tool, shading each technique by whether it's been hunted, already has a detection built, or has genuinely never been looked at by anyone.

A coverage gap isn't just a record-keeping detail. If Persistence techniques are well covered but nothing under Credential Access has ever been hunted, that unshaded gap itself becomes the next hypothesis, run straight through the hunting loop from Lesson 26.

Used this way, ATT&CK stops being something you only look up after the fact and becomes the actual map that decides what gets hunted next, systematically, rather than wherever an analyst's attention happens to land that day. Next: what happens once one of these hunts actually finds something real.
